An optimal composite interval index to produce remote-sensing time-series data

ABSTRACT

Complete remote-sensing time series with consistent length are important for obtaining reliable analytical results in regional applications. Temporal composite reconciles incomplete raw remote-sensing time series into a time series with fixed and equidistant time intervals, forming the basis for applications like crop classification. To our knowledge, no algorithms or indicators exist for determining the optimal composite interval while quantitatively considering cloud conditions and image acquisition capabilities across different latitudes. As a pioneering effort, we propose an optimal composite interval index (OCII) for producing remote-sensing composite time series. This index first calculates the proportion of valid (cloud-free) composite observations and the information loss from compositing, then describes the trade-off between these two aspects with a simple normalized difference form. We tested OCII using crop classification as an example, accessing classification accuracy with composite time-series data of varying intervals. Experimental results from three regions with different geographic conditions show that OCII suggested 16-day, 25-day and 30-day intervals for the sites with low cloud cover (37.56%), medium cloud cover (56.37%), and high cloud cover (82.11%), respectively. Classification accuracy was poor with either too short or too large composite intervals, and the optimal composite interval derived from OCII achieved a relative accuracy increase of 2.8–10.2%. This underscores the effectiveness of OCII considering differences in data availability at clear and cloudy sites. Calculating OCII requires only the data quality layer and can be easily implemented in various areas using the Google Earth Engine platform. We believe that OCII has great potential for crop classifications and other applications of remote-sensing time-series data.

Keywords:

  • Optical image time series
  • composite interval
  • temporal composition
  • optimal index

1. Introduction

High-frequency time-series data from Earth observation satellites play an irreplaceable role in monitoring dynamic changes of the Earth’s surface (Woodcock et al. Citation2020; Wulder et al. Citation2012). With the proliferation of Earth observation missions, time-series data from satellites such as MODIS, VIIRS (the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite), Landsat, Sentinel, and others are accumulating and becoming publicly accessible (Congalton Citation2018; Drusch et al. Citation2012; Friedl et al. Citation2002). Unfortunately, the actual acquisition of time-series data is frequently marred by discontinuities and time gaps due to cloud contamination and other interfering factors (Kovalskyy and Roy Citation2013; Santos et al. Citation2021; Sudmanns et al. Citation2020; Zhang et al. Citation2022). More importantly, these missing and incomplete data vary across regions and seasons because of different meteorological conditions and image acquisition capabilities at different latitudes (Wilson, Jetz, and Loreau Citation2016; Xu et al. Citation2022). To address these challenges, the process of reconciling these incomplete raw time-series data into a unified framework with fixed and equidistant time intervals, known as a temporal composite, has become a practical and widely accepted approach for producing standardized time-series data. This standardized time series can undergo further preprocessing (e.g. smooth; J. Chen et al. Citation2004; Y. Chen et al. Citation2021; Roy and Yan Citation2020) and be utilized in various applications, such as crop classification (Griffiths, Nendel, and Hostert Citation2019; You and Dong Citation2020).

Temporal composite has been commonly employed to obtain standard multi-day composite time-series products, such as the MODIS 16-day NDVI product (MOD13Q1, Didan et al. Citation2015; Wolfe, Roy, and Vermote Citation1998) and the Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) Leaf Area Index (LAI) product (Fuster et al. Citation2020). Additionally, temporal compositing has gained attraction in creating cloud-free and gap-filled time-series data with consistent and suitable temporal intervals for specific regional applications. The process of temporal compositing is moving a fixed window forward one by one interval to select the cloud-free and best-qualified values as the composite data for each temporal interval. There are two key steps involved. First, it is necessary to determine an appropriate composite interval, i.e. the composite window width. Next, if there is more than one cloud-free raw observation, the best-qualified values for each pixel within each composite interval are selected as the valid observation of composite data. Currently, various algorithms have been developed to assist in the selection or calculation of the best-qualified values (Francini et al. Citation2023). These algorithms include the Maximum Value Composite (MVC, Holben Citation1986), the Best Available Pixel algorithm (White et al. Citation2014), the Compositing based on Maximum ratio of Near Infrared to Blue band (MAX-RNB, Qiu et al. Citation2023), and the Moving Median Composite (Potapov, Turubanova, and Hansen Citation2011; You and Dong Citation2020). However, a significant challenge that persists is the determination of the composite interval. Currently, there is still a lack of established algorithms or indicators for determining the composite interval, and the current determination is often arbitrary and based on empirical knowledge.

The most important empirical knowledge for time-series composite is to reduce the missing data fraction as much as possible. Theoretically, for an ideal composite interval, we expect that there is at least one valid (cloud-free) observation for each pixel within each composite window. Meanwhile, the composite interval is equal to the temporal resolution of the composite data, which should maintain a higher temporal resolution. However, these two aspects are in competition. For example, a narrow composite interval offers a higher temporal resolution for the composite time series with less information loss of the raw time series. But on the other hand, a narrow interval makes it difficult to select cloud-free valid observations, as there is little scope for searching valid observations. Consequently, setting the composite interval involves a trade-off between rebuilding cloud-free time-series data and maintaining a high temporal resolution of the composite data. Particularly, how to describe the balance boundary of this trade-off using an intuitive numerical index should be discussed.

For temporal compositing, it is crucial to ensure that all pixels in the study areas have a consistent composite interval, so that subsequent processing methods are not affected by differences of time-series length in pixels. It is a common practice in existing studies to adhere to a uniform composite interval for time-series compositing regardless of a defined region. For example, previous studies empirically used a single composite interval on a global scale (Holben Citation1986; Tucker et al. Citation2005), which may lead to unsatisfactory quality of the derived composite time-series data due to non-uniform distribution of clouds and variations in image acquisition capabilities at different latitudes. Although CGLS offered LAI products with different composite windows on a global scale (Fuster et al. Citation2020), it remained unclear for users to determine which one is optimal in different sub-regions. Tian et al. (Citation2021) recognized the spatial variability of cloud frequency and proposed optimal composite intervals for the MVC in each 5°×5° sub-region of the northern hemisphere to improve the accuracy of phenology detection. However, their recommendations for optimal composite intervals used multi-year average cloud frequency ratios and were limited to 5°×5° sub-regions, restricting their applicability to more specific time periods and areas.

For global analyses, setting a fixed composite interval (e.g. 8 or 10 days) that ignores regional and seasonal characteristics is generally acceptable. However, for regional applications with specific time periods (Man et al. Citation2018; You and Dong Citation2020), setting different composite intervals by considering regional characteristics as well as differences in image acquisition capabilities becomes crucial for ensuring the quality of composite data and maintaining a high temporal resolution. Taking crop classification as an illustrative case, You and Dong (Citation2020) considered the spatial heterogeneity of data availability and examined how long the temporal interval should be set to obtain better accuracy of crop classification at a scale of one province in China. They generated time-series data with different composite windows and found that the performance of composite-based classification was sensitive to data availability across regions. However, this trial-and-error strategy heavily relied on pre-acquired crop samples and was only applicable to specific areas and periods. Therefore, it is very appealing to develop a simple and operational indicator to help determine optimal composite intervals in different regions.

In this study, we introduced an Optimal Composite Interval Index (OCII) for determining composite interval based on regional data availability. Compared to previous studies that rely on empirical knowledge, the OCII offers two key benefits. First, the OCII employs a numerical index, representing a pioneering attempt at quantifying the balance boundary of trade-off within determining composite interval. The OCII considers two aspects, the first is the proportion of valid observations in the composite time series, while the second is the potential information loss after compositing. Ideal composite time series requires both a high proportion of valid observations and sufficient temporal information. The two aspects quantitatively describe the positive effects (i.e. the increased proportion of valid observations resulting from a longer composite interval) and negative effects (i.e. the loss of temporal information associated with an extended composite interval) with increasing composite intervals. We combined the two aspects into the OCII to strike a balance between them. Second, the OCII has a simple form without relying on local prior assumptions or auxiliary data exploration, allowing it to provide corresponding optimal composite interval recommendations for various regions. To validate the effectiveness of the OCII, we tested it at three representative sites that varied in size and cloud cover. The results illustrated how the OCII balances positive and negative effects. We further compared its quantitative performances in crop classification using the optimal composite interval recommended by OCII with that of other intervals.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. The development of OCII

The OCII is an indicator to determine the composite interval (e.g. most commonly 8, 10, 16, 30, or 60 days) for optical reflectance/vegetation index time-series data. We assumed that a better composite interval should have a larger proportion of valid observations in composite time series and meanwhile have a lower information loss due to the composite operations. Following this assumption, the two aspects quantitatively in OCII are the following.

First, for a composite time series with a given composite interval, we calculated the Proportion of Valid Observations for the i-th pixel in the composite time series (referred to as PVOi), namely as the ratio of valid observations to the length of the composite time series:

(1) PVOi=valid_numicom/L(1)

where L is the number of composite intervals in the length of the time series under a predefined composite interval, valid_numicom represents the number of valid observations in composite L for the i-th pixel. It is conceivable that larger composite interval may have higher PVO value because it is easier to search valid observations in larger composite windows. For a study area, data availability of each pixel is not the same due to the random appearance of cloud. To represent the majority of the area, the pixel-level PVOi values were averaged to the area-level as:

(2) PVO=∑i=1NPVOiN(2)

where N is the total number of pixels in the study area.

Secondly, the composite operation with a wider composite window may lead to a decrease in the number of composite intervals in the length of the composite time series, suggesting a decrease in temporal resolution with the potential loss of information. This effect was quantified by comparing the total number of valid observations in the composite time series to that in the raw time series. Information Loss of Composite for the i-th pixel (ILCi) was expressed as:

(3) ILCi=valid_numiraw−valid_numicom/valid_numiraw(3)

where valid_numiraw represents the number of valid observations in raw time series. Likewise, the ILCi values of all pixels in a study area were averaged to generate the area-level ILC value.

For a better composite interval, we expected a higher proportion of valid observations (i.e. a larger PVO value) and a less potential information loss (a smaller ILC value). However, the two aspects competed with each other and cannot achieve optimal results simultaneously. To account for the trade-off between PVO and ILC, OCII calculated the difference between them, expressed as:

(4) OCII=PVOnormalize−ILCnormalizedatanormalize=data−datamindatamax−datamin(4)

Here, the normalized forms of PVO and ILC (PVOnormalize and ILCnormalize) were used because the two components have different ranges of values. The PVO and ILC represent positive and negative aspects of composite interval increases, respectively, so as the composite interval increases, OCII first increases due to the greater influence of PVO and then decreases due to the greater influence of ILC. The highest OCII value is usually found at a value in the middle part of a predefined set of possible intervals (see in section 4). As the first attempt, OCII provides a simple approach to select the optimal compositing temporal interval, eliminating the need for trial-and-error exploration.

2.2. Study area

Because the dynamics of optical signals from crops are relatively complex and thus sensitive to the compositing interval, we tested the effectiveness of OCII for crop mapping at three study sites, which are predominantly croplands (). The first site is located in Yili County, Xinjiang, China, covering an area of 2,700 km2 and having maize and spring wheat as its main crops. The second site is the state of Iowa, U.S.A., with an area of about 145,000 km2 and is mainly planted with maize and soybeans. The third site is a cloudy area in the Sichuan Basin of China, covering about 60,000 km2, and the main spring crops are winter wheat and rapeseed. The target crops in classification experiments vary with testing sites (i.e. spring wheat, maize, and other small-field crops in Yili site, maize and soybean in Iowa site, and rapeseed and winter wheat in Sichuan site), which represent common crop dynamics. Moreover, data availability at the three testing sites is completely different. According to the Global 1-km Cloud Cover product (Wilson, Jetz, and Loreau Citation2016), the annual cloud frequencies for the testing sites in Yili, Iowa and Sichuan are 37.56%, 56.37% and 82.11%, representing low, medium, and high cloud coverage, respectively. Such significant differences in cloud coverages allow us to fully evaluate the performance of OCII.

Figure 1. Location and overview of the three study sites. In the experiment of crop mapping, we collected crop samples from the sub-region areas at each site (red rectangle) to avoid overfitting.

2.3. Satellite images

We collected Sentinel-2A&B level-2 surface reflectance (SR) imagery, which has an atmospheric correction applied to Top-Of-Atmosphere Level-1C orthoimage products, during the growing season of major crops from the Google Earth Engine platform at the three testing sites (). clearly shows significant differences in the number of good observations at the three testing sites. Cloud-covered pixels were identified by the quality flags, which are pixels with values of 3, 9, or 10 in the Scene CLassification flags, or values greater than 65 in the S2_CLOUD_PROBABILITY product (Skakun et al. Citation2022). The OCII was solely calculated based on the cloud flags. gives detailed information of the images used for the three testing sites.

Table 1. Sentinel-2 image information at three sites. The number of scenes covering the study site and the regional averaged cloud-free (good) observations (obs.) in the target period were counted.

3. Experiments

Quantitative assessments using composite time series with different intervals for crop classification at each testing site were conducted. We generated the composite time series with eight possible composite intervals (i.e. most commonly 8, 10, 16, 20, 25, 30, 60, and 90 days). An optimal composite interval can be suggested by OCII for each testing site. To determine the composite value in each composite interval, two compositing algorithms were considered for more comprehensive evaluation of OCII. One is the widely used median compositing algorithm, which is less affected by extreme outliers and has high computational efficiency (Teluguntla et al. Citation2018; You and Dong Citation2020). The other is the recently developed MAX-RNB compositing algorithm, which selects the value with the maximum Ratio of NIR to Blue reflectance within each composite window and was reported to be less affected by data noise (clouds, clouds shadows, snow/ice, and haze) (Qiu et al. Citation2023).

For crop classification based on composite time-series data of different intervals, crop samples were collected from the corresponding reference crop maps. For non-crop samples (e.g. built-up areas, water bodies, and bare lands), we collected them according to ESA WorldCover 2021 (Zanaga et al. Citation2022). Training crop samples were randomly selected from specific sub-regions within the study area, while validation samples were randomly chosen from the entire area outside these sub-regions, ensuring no overlap between the two. The reference crop map at the Iowa site containing the target crops, maize and soybeans, was collected from the Cropland Data Layer (CDL), which is provided by the United States Department of Agriculture and was reported to have an overall accuracy of greater than 90% (Boryan et al. Citation2011; Lark, Schelly, and Gibbs Citation2021). Winter wheat and rapeseed are the target crops for Sichuan site. The reference crop map at the Sichuan site was obtained from the winter wheat map provided by Dong et al. (Citation2020), which has producer’s and user’s accuracy higher than 89.30 % and 90.59 %, and the rapeseed map provided by Zang et al. (Citation2023) with an average overall accuracy of 94.90%. The reference crop map at the Yili site containing spring wheat and maize were provided by local agricultural research institutions and were generated through visual interpretation of remotely sensed data and intensive field surveys. In brief, the accuracy of above used reference maps have been well evaluated by relevant studies to be above 90%, and the training and validation samples obtained from them are reliable and accurate.

We used a random forests (RF) model to conduct the composite-based crop classification experiment. Random Forest classifier is an ensemble learning method that is efficient, simple to parametrize, robust, and often used for crop type and cropping pattern mapping (Feyisa et al. Citation2020). Considering the comparison of different composite intervals (i.e. 8, 10, 16, 20, 25, 30, 60, and 90 days), eight random forest classification scenarios were done based on same crop samples at each testing site. To avoid overfitting the RF model, a sub-to-whole classification approach was adopted, where training samples were taken not randomly from the entire region, but from one specific sub-region (as shown in the red blocks of each site in ). The trained classifier was then applied to the whole region to obtain crop maps. Accuracy validation was done throughout the whole region. Because we selected three sub-regions at each site, one classification result can be obtained using each of the three sub-regions and the final classification accuracy was calculated as the average of the three classification results.

The input features in the RF model included both composite surface reflectance time series (i.e. green, red, two red edges, near-infrared, and two short wave infrared reflectance bands) and the composite NDVI time series. For each classification scenario at each site, the only difference is the composite interval of input features. Considering the balance between accuracy and computational efficiency, we set the minimum size of a terminal node as 10 and the number of decision trees as 100 in the RF model. Classification accuracy was evaluated by the F1-score, which better assesses the accuracy of each class rather than the overall accuracy.

4. Results

4.1. Qualitative assessment of OCII

The PVO and ILC constitute the two components in the OCII. Therefore, we showed the change patterns of PVO, ILC, and OCII with the increase in composite intervals at the three testing sites (). At the Yili site, the PVO value rapidly reaches a high value of 0.8 at the 16-day composite interval and then increases only slightly after this composite interval; however, the ILC value exhibits a different change pattern with a continuous increase up to the 90-day interval. Therefore, for the Yili site where the percentage of clear days is relatively high, the peak value of OCII occurs at the16-day composite interval (). At the Iowa site, PVO and ILC values have a relatively uniform increase until the 25-day interval. Beyond this point, the increase in ILC exceeds that of PVO, suggesting the peak of OCII at the 25-day interval. At the cloudy Sichuan site, the PVO value increases continuously due to the limited availability of valid data, and the increase speed of ILC exceeds that of PVO after the 30-day interval. As a result, the OCII value reaches its highest value at 30 days.

Figure 2. The changes of normalized PVO, normalized ILC, and OCII under different composite intervals.

Furthermore, we examined the composite images at four separate dates throughout growing seasons using different composite intervals (). The four dates are Jan. 1 April 20011 June 200130, and 28 September 2020 for the Yili and Iowa sites and Sep. 1 December 200101, 1 March 2020, and 30 May 2021 for the Sichuan site. At the Yili site, most pixels have valid composite values even for narrow composite intervals. However, when the composite intervals are larger than 16-day, we observed that some areas remain green on Sep. 28 (e.g. see the red box in ), which does not align with the low NDVI values on this date due to maize harvests. At the Iowa site, composite images with intervals larger than 25-day all have high portions of valid observations (). The composite images on Sep. 28 with large 60/90-day composite intervals exhibit obvious coverages of green vegetation, and this is not consistent with the harvest characteristics of maize and soybeans. At Sichuan site, for intervals shorter than 30-day, there are still serious missing values in the composite images (). For the composition of Sentinel-2 time-series data, OCII provides a simple and operational criterion and suggests a small composite interval (16-day) for the Yili site and larger intervals (25-day and 30-day) for the cloudy Iowa and Sichuan sites, respectively.

Figure 3. The composite images (true colour) with different composite intervals at Yili site. Four separate dates (Jan. 01, Apr. 01, Jun. 30, and Sep. 28, 2020) throughout growing seasons are shown here.

4.2. Application assessments of OCII in crop classification

We performed the quantitative assessments of OCII for the crop classification application. shows the classification accuracy (F1-score) for main crops at the three testing sites under different composite intervals. shows the classification maps at the three testing sites under small interval (8-day), optimal interval, and large interval (90-day). Both the median composition and MAX-RNB algorithms were used to generate the composition value in each interval. When using the median composition algorithm, at the Yili site, the classification accuracy of the main crops (spring wheat and maize) is relatively high under the OCII-derived 16-day composite interval and obviously decreases for composite intervals larger than 20–25 day (). At the Iowa site, the highest F1-score values are achieved for both maize and soybean using the OCII-derived 25-day composite interval (). At the Sichuan site, there is also relatively good performance of crop classification for winter wheat and rapeseed under the OCII-derived 30-day composite interval (). Similar results were achieved by using the MAX-RNB compositing (right column in ). Interestingly, we found that both the Iowa and Sichuan sites had less accurate classification compared to the OCII-derived crop classification under either small composite intervals (for example, 8 days) or large composite intervals (>60 days). Regarding the classification maps, we found that at the Iowa site, the classification map produced by 8-day composite images showed salt-and-pepper noise, and obvious omission error existed in the classification map when 90-day composite interval was adopted. At the Sichuan site, rapeseed is misclassified as winter wheat using either a small composite interval (8-day) or a larger interval (90-day). The OCII-derived crop classification maps are more consistent with the reference maps ().

Figure 6. Changes in F1-scores of crop classification under different composite intervals at the three testing sites (a-c). The left and right columns are the results using the median compositing algorithm and the MAX-RNB algorithm, respectively. The red dashed line represents the optimal compositing interval determined by OCII.

Figure 7. Classification maps of the three testing sites under different composite intervals (i.e. small interval (8-day), optimal interval, and large interval (90-day)).

The performance of crop classification is affected by the determination of composite intervals. In the case of small composite time intervals, poor classification performance (lower F1-score values) may be attributed to severe data gaps in the composite time series. On the other hand, if the composite interval is too large, the loss of critical crop phenological information may be responsible for the lower classification accuracy. For example, at the Iowa site, the 60-day composite images on Sep. 28 lost important harvest characteristics using such a wide-interval composite (as shown in true colour in ). The OCII effectively balances the proportion of valid observations with the potential loss of information, producing composite time series suitable for practical applications.

5. Discussion

5.1. The effect of temporal distribution of valid observations on OCII

The item of PVO in OCII considers the proportion of valid observations in the composite time series (EquationEquation 1(1) PVOi=valid_numicom/L(1) ). However, the temporal distribution of valid observations may be also considered to describe annual changes in land surface. Why not include the temporal distribution of valid observations into OCII? We explain this through the strong correlation between PVO and the temporal distribution of valid observations. As the composite interval increases, the composite time series has higher PVO values, lower temporal resolution, and meanwhile more uniform temporal distributions. Thus, the inclusion of a temporal distribution indicator contributes relatively limited information to the optimal composite interval index. To validate this explanation, here we used a widely used Gini index to measure the uniformity of composite time series and investigated the relationship between Gini index values and PVO values under eight different intervals for each testing site (). In a brief way, the Gini index quantifies the uniformity of composite time series by comparing the actual Lorenz curve (i.e. the attribute value is the interval between each pair of valid observation dates) with an ideal Lorenz curve (i.e. absolute equal intervals for each observation) (Ortega et al. Citation1991). Both the PVO and the Gini index were averaged over all pixels in each study area. The Gini index ranges from 0 to 1, with smaller values indicating more uniform data distributions. We used the 1-Gini form for more intuitive comparisons with the PVO index. As we expected, there are strong linear correlations between the PVO values and the 1-Gini values at all three testing sites (R2 >0.98 in ), suggesting that it is unnecessary to include temporal distribution information (e.g. Gini index).

Figure 8. The correlation between area-level PVO index and 1-Gini index at three testing sites. Red points represent the different composite interval.

5.2. Land cover types impact

The calculation of OCII is simple and requires the data quality layer only. Because of the different complexity of spectral annual changes for different land covers, one may concern why not generate the composite time series according to land cover types? For example, OCII can be calculated by using the pixels of a given land cover type only instead of all pixels in the region. We interpret this to mean that the availability of raw data plays a dominant role in generating composite time series. Considering smaller composite intervals for each land cover type will neglect real data availability, leading to missing data and inconsistent lengths of time series in regional applications. For example, at the cloudy Sichuan site, a smaller composite interval cannot improve the classification accuracy for crops with complex spectral annual changes due to the limitations in the availability of valid data. In addition, precise land cover information is often unknown or unavailable prior to performing the composite task. Accordingly, it is unnecessary to consider land cover types in OCII to ensure that composite time series should have a consistent interval for all pixels in practical applications.

5.3. Uncertainties in OCII

First, accurate cloud and cloud shadow detection is crucial for time series composition. Uncertainty in the cloud mask may introduce bias into the calculation of OCII. The compositing algorithms (e.g. median composition) can reduce the effect of some omitted clouds and cloud shadows on the composited time series. Therefore, decreasing commission error in the cloud mask may improve the performance of OCII. Second, some particular application scenarios may focus more on either PVO or ILC. For example, more dense time series may be required in the applications of land cover change detection or land surface disturbance (e.g. fire) monitoring. Nearly cloud free images during specific crop growing season may be crucial for crop classification. For these objectives, it may increase the weights of ILC or the weights of PVO in the calculation of OCII (i.e. Equation 4). However, the determinations of weights are case dependent and require prior knowledge (e.g. the time scale of disturbance occurrence, or the crop calendar). Third, OCII was tested by using the median and the recently MAX-RNB algorithms to generate the composite value in each interval. The generally consistent experimental results in the assessments of OCII for crop classification suggest the robustness of this proposed index. Fourth, overlapping areas between adjacent swaths often exhibit higher observation frequencies. For these regions, finer sub-areas can be delineated within the overlapping zones. By calculating the OCII using only the pixels within these sub-areas, we can generate vegetation index (VI) time-series data with smaller compositing intervals tailored to these sub-areas. This may enhance the suitability of the data for specific applications within these particular sub-areas.

Considering these uncertainties of determining composite interval, future research may be focus on the following aspects to balance the PVO and ILC in OCII more intricately: To tailor the optimal composite interval index for complex applications, crafting appropriate weights is essential; using OCII with more composite algorithms is theoretically applicable and may be adopted in future studies; With the data-driven property of OCII, it presents an opportunity to generate composite datasets for crop classification, using different satellite sources like MODIS and Landsat, and for analysing more complex agricultural systems, such as smaller, fragmented crop fields.

6. Conclusions

Raw optical time-series data are usually incomplete and inconsistent across areas due to cloud contamination. The initial and crucial step in utilizing this data for time-series applications is to generate composite time series with an equal and uniform time interval. Unfortunately, the current practice of determining composite intervals is often based on empirical knowledge without specific algorithms or indicators. This study addresses this critical research gap by introducing an OCII to produce the composite time series of remote sensing images. The OCII considers the balance between positive aspect and negative aspect. In our case studies based on Sentinel-2 composite time series, OCII determines the optimal composite interval as the time interval exhibiting the highest OCII value based on different data availability for a given study region, which are 16-day for Yili site (with 37.56% cloud cover), 25-day for Iowa site (with 56.37% cloud cover), and 30-day for Sichuan site (with 82.11% cloud cover). Quantitatively assessments in our cases show that the composite time series generated based on the OCII-derived composite interval can generate relatively high crop classification accuracy at both clear and cloudy testing sites; the composite intervals selected by OCII can provide a classification accuracy improvement of at least 2.8% and up to 10.2% compared to either smaller or larger composite intervals. The OCII offers a simple form, with its calculation relying solely on the data quality layer. The selection of an appropriate composite interval for producing remote sensing time series is an ongoing challenge in the research community. We expect that the proposed OCII can be a useful tool for users working with remote sensing time-series data.
